to_title: Greek gods as archetypes (c. 8th c. BCE)
note: spirits become named gods with characters

check_1.note: Source opened only says Greek religion kept animistic elements; the spirits-to-gods sequence is an older evolutionary scheme, not stated outright.

check_2.note: Greek religion included spirits and anthropomorphic gods, but no source established the proposed historical transformation.

note: the soul as the organising form of a living body

check_1.note: No source found saying Aristotle's hylomorphic soul builds on animism; thematic parallel only.

check_2.note: Aristotle's hylomorphic soul is documented; descent from prehistoric animism is not.

to_title: Plato: forms and the cave (c. 375 BCE)
note: a disputed Pythagorean influence on Plato's metaphysics and mathematics

check_1.note: Marked Pythagorean influence on Plato is stated; page adds that the world of forms itself is Platonic, not Pythagorean.

check_2.note: Pythagorean influence was limited; SEP calls inferring it from Plato's mathematics a serious mistake and does not derive his core Forms from it.

note: the stoics made logos the rational order of the cosmos

check_1.note: Stoics: logos as active reason pervading and animating the universe.

check_2.note: Heraclitean and Stoic logos are a standard historical connection, though the opened pages did not explicitly state direct influence.

note: immaterial soul becomes res cogitans

check_1.note: SEP Dualism traces Christian adoption of Platonic soul-dualism before Descartes but does not state the derivation explicitly.

check_2.note: Descartes styled himself a Christian philosopher and pursued the Church-backed project of proving the soul's immateriality.

note: la mettrie extends descartes' animal-machine to humans and drops the soul

check_1.note: Extends Descartes' animal-automaton argument to humans and denies a separate soul; so it both builds on and opposes Descartes.

check_2.note: La Mettrie extends machine language to feeling animals and humans while making soul a material brain function.

note: the rationalist side kant tries to reconcile

check_1.note: Kant studied Leibniz and Wolff, then criticised Leibnizian-Wolffian rationalism; so partly against as well as builds.

check_2.note: SEP documents Leibniz's influence and the conventional account of Kant navigating Leibnizian rationalism and Humean empiricism.

note: ethics as calculation

check_1.note: Bentham's cited influences (Helvetius, Beccaria, Hume) are Enlightenment figures, but no opened page states the link in these words.

check_2.note: Bentham's calculative ethics belongs to the late Enlightenment, but no opened source explicitly established this broad developmental link.

to_title: Michael Levin: bioelectricity and collective intelligence (2019)
note: cells as agents that cooperate to build bodies

check_1.note: No source found tying Levin's work to cell theory; cell theory does not treat cells as cooperating agents.

check_2.note: Levin documents cooperative cellular agency and body-building, but no source tied this specifically to historical cell theory.

note: 'we will never know' returns a century later

check_1.note: Thematic parallel; pages opened name Leibniz and Huxley as precursors, not du Bois-Reymond. No influence shown.

check_2.note: The source explicitly calls McGinn the contemporary continuator of du Bois-Reymond's unknowability claim.

to_title: William James: The Principles of Psychology (1890)
note: psychology becomes a laboratory science

check_1.note: Pages opened name Wundt as founder of experimental psychology and James teaching it from 1875, but do not link them directly.

check_2.note: The source discusses James's teaching laboratory and Wundt's permanent research laboratory in psychology's institutionalization as laboratory science.

note: behaviorism made observable behaviour, rather than introspection, its primary evidence

check_1.note: Behaviorism rejected introspection; page warns Wundt's own view is often misread, and Skinner's radical behaviorism treated introspection as behavior.

check_2.note: Skinner explicitly said radical behaviorism restores introspection and does not deny self-observation; the note fits Watson better than Skinner.

note: logic as the form of language

check_1.note: Wittgenstein read Frege, visited him in 1911; Frege sent him to Russell. The note's wording is a gloss.

check_2.note: Wittgenstein acknowledged Frege and inherited his function-argument analysis and conception of logic's relation to language.

note: a formal definition of truth

check_1.note: SEP's Tarski and Tarski-truth entries do not mention Frege; any influence is indirect.

check_2.note: The historical study presents Frege's rigorous semantics as a close precursor to Tarski's formal truth theories.

to_title: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (1985)
note: lisp and scheme

check_1.note: Scheme has lambda calculus at its core and is the language used with SICP.

check_2.note: SICP uses Scheme, whose first-class procedures derive from lambda calculus, but no single reliable opened source stated the complete link.

to_title: John von Neumann and the first computers (1837–1956)
note: the stored-program computer

check_1.note: Von Neumann credited the fundamental conception to Turing; Eckert and Mauchly were unaware of Turing's work.

check_2.note: Von Neumann knew Turing's universal machine, but historians dispute whether it influenced his stored-program architecture.

note: 'can machines think?'

check_1.note: History pages present Turing's 1950 paper as a precursor to the 1956 founding, but do not state that the workshop drew on it.

check_2.note: Stanford's AI history says Turing's 1950 essay inspired AI and anticipated machine intelligence and learning before Dartmouth.

note: information and compression as a theory of induction

check_1.note: Algorithmic information theory, founded by Solomonoff, is described as Shannon plus Turing; no page ties Solomonoff induction itself to Shannon.

check_2.note: Solomonoff explicitly says Shannon's information theory profoundly shaped his induction ideas through probability and information packing.

note: learning as compression

check_1.note: Schmidhuber's own page presents his generalized Kolmogorov complexity work as extending Solomonoff's algorithmic probability and universal prediction.

check_2.note: The intellectual lineage is standard, but the opened sources did not explicitly connect Solomonoff to Schmidhuber's compression-learning program.

note: prediction and compression

check_1.note: Predictive text compression (PPM, arithmetic coding) rests on Shannon's theory; no opened page states Witten's debt in so many words.

check_2.note: Witten's compression and induction work fits Shannon's framework, but no opened source explicitly stated this influence.

from_title: John von Neumann and the first computers (1837–1956)
note: reliable computing from unreliable parts

check_1.note: Thematic link to von Neumann's 1956 unreliable-components paper; found no reliable source stating Ackley builds on it.

note: simple rules, complex behaviour

from_title: John von Neumann and the first computers (1837–1956)
note: the universe as a cellular automaton

note: if physics is computation it could be run

check_1.note: Page says digital physics overlaps with but is distinct from the simulation hypothesis.

check_2.note: Digital physics and simulation are related but logically distinct; neither implies the other.

note: information as more basic than matter

check_1.note: Page lists Wheeler's 'it from bit' as the informational-primacy strand, influential beyond digital physics.

check_2.note: Both make information fundamental, but the opened source did not explicitly place Wheeler's proposal within digital physics.

note: unlimited complexity from a tiny rule

check_1.note: Thematic parallel only; no source read discusses the two together.

note: neural nets, then minsky's critique of them

check_1.note: Minsky named as a student inspired by McCulloch and Pitts; built SNARC in 1951, later co-wrote Perceptrons.

check_2.note: The neural-network lineage and Minsky's later critique are standard, but no opened source stated this specific two-part connection.

note: second-order cybernetics

check_1.note: Autopoiesis is listed among the developments of second-order cybernetics. Covers the autopoiesis half of the point only.

check_2.note: Autopoiesis is standardly associated with second-order cybernetics, but the opened primary sources did not explicitly state that lineage.

note: what keeps a living system ordered

check_1.note: Page says autopoiesis and related theories of life found their original inspiration in Schrödinger's What Is Life?

check_2.note: Both address living order, but no opened reliable source documented Schrödinger as a source for autopoiesis.

note: pattern matching that feels like understanding

check_1.note: Page calls ELIZA a symbolic AI chatbot whose basic text processing convinced users of understanding.

check_2.note: ELIZA plainly uses symbolic pattern rules, but the opened original paper did not label it as building on symbolic AI.

note: a crowd of demons becomes a society of mind

check_1.note: Wikipedia says Minsky considered Selfridge a mentor; lineage widely told, but no reliable page read states the debt outright.

check_2.note: The parallel-agent resemblance is strong, but opened sources did not securely document Pandemonium as the direct source of Society of Mind.

note: the transformer

check_1.note: LLMs are typically based on the transformer neural network architecture.

check_2.note: Transformers are deep neural architectures and underpin modern LLMs, but the opened original paper did not itself discuss LLMs.

to_title: Chollet: On the Measure of Intelligence (2019)
note: skill is not intelligence

check_1.note: Chollet argues against measuring intelligence by task skill; calling the paper 'against deep learning' is a judgement call.

note: learned cellular automata

check_1.note: The paper cites Conway's Game of Life and its continuous generalisations (SmoothLife, Lenia) as inspiration.

check_2.note: Neural cellular automata extend the cellular-automaton paradigm, but the opened paper did not explicitly derive its method from Conway's Life.

from_title: Dreyfus: What Computers Still Can't Do (1972 / 1992)
note: heidegger against the symbol-crunching mind

check_1.note: IEP lists Dreyfus among critiques embodied theorists take up; Wikipedia calls views similar. Explicit 'builds on' not found.

to_title: AI risk: Bostrom, Yudkowsky and the doom debate (2003–2023)
note: runaway self-improvement

check_1.note: Page ties the intelligence explosion to existential risk and AI-alignment research (MIRI, FHI).

check_2.note: Recursive self-improvement connects singularity scenarios to modern AI-risk arguments, but the specific lineage is broader than one source.

to_title: Materialism and physicalism (ancient; modern form 20th c.)
note: man a machine

check_1.note: Described as a work of materialist philosophy; La Mettrie is part of the tradition rather than a source of modern physicalism.

check_2.note: Routledge identifies L’Homme machine as a materialist manifesto applying materialism explicitly to human beings.

from_title: Materialism and physicalism (ancient; modern form 20th c.)
note: what matters is organisation, not stuff

check_1.note: SEP: functionalism is officially neutral between materialism and dualism, though attractive to materialists; arose as an alternative to identity theory. 'Builds' is a judgement.

check_2.note: Functionalism commonly develops within physicalist philosophy of mind, though it is not logically committed to physicalism.

note: multiple realisability comes from universal computation

check_1.note: Turing machines inspired Putnam's machine functionalism; sources do not derive multiple realisability from universal computation specifically.

check_2.note: SEP says Turing’s work was explicitly invoked and inspired Putnam’s machine-state theories in early functionalism.

to_title: Ned Block: access vs phenomenal consciousness (1995)
note: 'troubles with functionalism'

check_1.note: Block's China brain and inverted qualia objections; this is his 1978 work, not the 1995 access/phenomenal paper.

check_2.note: SEP discusses Block’s absent-qualia and Chinese-nation objections as major challenges to functionalism.

note: dennett's functionalist account of consciousness

check_1.note: Dennett calls himself a 'teleofunctionalist' in Consciousness Explained.

check_2.note: Dennett’s consciousness theory is routinely classified as broadly functionalist, though his account is not reducible to generic functionalism.

note: models are simplifications, not the thing

check_1.note: Symposium paper: Chirimuuta argues against the literal interpretation of computational models; target is computationalism in neuroscience more than functionalism generally.

check_2.note: The review says Chirimuuta rejects inferring machine consciousness by mistaking computational models for the brain they simplify.

from_title: Nagel: What Is It Like to Be a Bat? (1974)
note: 'what it is like' becomes the hard problem

check_1.note: Chalmers uses Nagel's 'what it is like' definition of consciousness.

check_2.note: Nagel’s what-it-is-like formulation is a standard precursor to Chalmers’s hard problem, but direct dependence is not established here.

note: from gap to hard problem

check_1.note: Bridging the explanatory gap 'is known as the hard problem'.

check_2.note: The explanatory gap is a standard precursor to the hard problem, though Chalmers’s argument is not simply Levine’s renamed.

note: the mill argument is the hard problem in 1714

check_1.note: Sources name Leibniz's mill as a precursor of the hard problem; none says Chalmers drew on it. 'Related' would be documented.

check_2.note: Leibniz’s mill anticipates an explanatory concern, but calling it the hard problem in 1714 is retrospective interpretation.

note: walking around inside the machine and finding no understanding

check_1.note: Leibniz's mill is listed as a precursor argument to the Chinese room.

check_2.note: The mill and Chinese room are commonly compared as internal-observer arguments, but differ in target and conclusion.
